levels.text: An official record or primary document: the survey sheets, government archives, Hansard, a census.
Contemporary press, an encyclopedia or careful secondary work.
One person's testimony, an organisation about itself, or a popular figure nobody has traced.
Worked out by this project from documented material: measured on the survey sheets or on the model.
A reasoned estimate where nothing is recorded, such as storey counts from a rule checked against photographs.
Drawn to show what was typical, not a record: façade colours, rooftop clutter, room layouts, furniture.

method.title: The plan
method.text: Every building outline, address number, street name and landmark is traced from the Lands Department's survey sheet 11-NE-11A of May 1987, the last to map the city plot by plot; the Yamen from the 2024 sheet.

method.title: Heights
method.text: Storeys follow a rule based on each plot's size and position, checked against Ian Lambot's 1989 aerial photograph (four buildings counted) and the archive claims (floors named); about 13–14 storeys at most, the limit enforced from 1975.

method.title: The ground
method.text: A smooth surface fitted to the survey's spot heights: the city fell about 9 m from north-west to south-east.

method.title: Rooms and businesses
method.text: About 400 clearance claims in the Government Records Service give a business, an address and a floor; they are placed in their buildings. Every other unit's use, and all room layouts, are illustrative.

method.title: Day, night and vice
method.text: The sun follows 14 January 1987, the day the city was surveyed. The crime and vice layers show what sources say for each era, marked by certainty; no den or brothel locations are recorded, so none are drawn.

method.title: Economy
method.text: Trades and floors are counted from the clearance claims; rents, compensation and water from the sources cited.

method.title: Growth
method.text: From 1961 to 1987, each plot is checked on every survey sheet: is its outline drawn, is it drawn with the heavy line of a permanent building (from 1975), and is it marked CIP, construction in progress. This dates the drawings, not the buildings.

method.title: Daylight
method.text: How much sky each lane spot and wall can see is measured on the model; it rests on the inferred heights.

method.title: Places to step inside
method.text: The flat, the dentist's, the fish-ball workshop, the kaifong office, the rooftop and the school are illustrations of what was typical, with every object marked by certainty and the sources cited where they exist.

method.title: Photographs
method.text: Only open-licensed photographs from Wikimedia Commons are shown, each credited. Copyrighted photographs used in research are linked, not reproduced.

method.title: Residents' voices
method.text: Former residents' words are short quotations from published interviews, translated here and always linked to the original; videos play from YouTube only when you press play.

method.title: Photo style
method.text: The places' photo style dresses the same models in scanned real-world surfaces (plaster, terrazzo, timber, steel) and light from real places, all CC0 from Poly Haven; on desktops it can ray-trace the view. It makes the rooms look real, not more certain: what each object is and why it is there still carries its own badge.

facts.claim: Area of the walled city site
Other area figures: 6.5 acres (Lords 1974), 2.7 ha (SCMP), 'little more than 7 acres / 2.8 ha' (Wikipedia urban section), about 26,000 m2 (HK01)
facts.note: Measure it ourselves from the 1987 survey sheet in Phase 1

facts.claim: Plan dimensions of the site
Plan dimensions given by the SCMP graphic
Approximate centre in HK1980 Grid; the 1:1000 sheet covering the city is 11-NE-11A (E 837,500-838,250, N 821,000-821,600)
facts.note: Refine from the survey sheet crops in Phase 1

facts.claim: Kai Tak airport lay about 800 m south of the city
The Qing wall was about 4 m tall and 4.6 m thick, with four entrances
facts.note: UPI 1984 gives a 13-foot wall

facts.claim: The Japanese occupation force dismantled the wall and used the stone to extend Kai Tak airport
Surviving remnants: the Yamen (built 1847) and the South Gate foundations and two granite plaques ('South Gate', 'Kowloon Walled City') unearthed in 1994; both declared monuments on 4 Oct 1996
The park's paths and pavilions are named after streets and buildings of the walled city
facts.note: Useful to recover street names and positions

facts.claim: Number of buildings at peak
Other building counts: 300 (Wikipedia 1960s section), 503 in 1994 (park article, uncited)
facts.note: Counts depend on what counts as one building; Phase 1 will count footprints on the 1987 sheet

facts.claim: A height limit of 13-14 storeys applied because of the Kai Tak approach
Authorities began enforcing the height limit in 1975; two buildings lost their top floors
Buildings on the alleys were 10, 11 and up to 13 storeys
Most buildings were between 10 and 14 storeys
In 1963 buildings were only 1-2 storeys and alleys were 8-10 ft of mud
facts.note: Compare with the 1961-1974 1:600 survey sheets

facts.claim: After a 1963 clearance attempt was stopped by Chinese protest, speculators built the enclave up
Towers were built without architects or engineers, outside building and sanitation rules; many had poor or no foundations
A typical unit was about 23 m2
Living space per person
Buildings almost touched: neighbours passed food across, and facing windows could not both open
Upper-level stairs and passages ran so far that one could cross the city north to south without touching the ground
Residents crossed a plank over an alley at the 10th storey to visit neighbours
Caged balconies and rooftop additions covered the facades
Alleys were often only 1-2 m wide, poorly lit and drained
No alley was wider than about 3 ft; most were 2 ft and some 18 in; they were unpaved earth with an open drain down the middle, and no wheeled vehicle could enter
facts.note: Probably the narrowest passages; main lanes were wider

facts.claim: On survey day officials cordoned the 83 streets and alleys leading into the city
facts.note: Unclear whether 83 counts entrances or all lanes; HK01 says about 20 streets

facts.claim: Street names printed inside the city on the May 1987 survey: Lung Chun Road (south edge, numbers to 160), West City Road (west edge), Tai Chang Street (two arms), Sz Kung Street, Alms House Back Street, Lo Yan Street, Tin Hau Temple Street, Kwong Ming Street, Lung Shing Road
facts.note: Chinese names to confirm from the park plan (commons-plan); likely 龍津道, 西城路, 大井街, 老人街, 天后廟街, 光明街, 龍城路

facts.claim: HK01 interviewees place the vice trade on Lung Shing Road 龍城路 and Kwong Ming Street 光明街

Features marked on the May 1987 survey: the H-shaped former Yamen labelled 'School', a clinic beside it, a temple on Tin Hau Temple Street, several shrines ('Shr'), wells ('W'), two public latrines ('Lat'), a footbridge ('FB'), an electric transformer ('ET') at the south edge, temporary structures ('TS') and a garden along the east side
facts.note: Every building outline carries its address number(s): the base for Phase 1 tracing

facts.claim: Roads outside the city: Tung Tau Tsuen Road 東頭村道 on the north (dentists' frontage), Tung Tsing Road 東正道 on the east, Carpenter Road 賈炳達道 on the south

sources.loc: 1991 caption: dental clinics at an edge

facts.claim: Sai Tau Tsuen squatter village south and west of the city was cleared in 1985 for Carpenter Road Park; outsiders often mistook it for part of the city
Eight freshwater standpipes: one inside the city and seven around its perimeter

sources.loc: Urban settlement: eight municipal pipes (Goddard 2007 pp36-38)

facts.claim: Street taps stood only at the outer edge, on Tung Tau Tsuen Road and Tung Tsing Road; piping into the city was judged infeasible
77 wells, some about 90 m deep; electric pumps lifted water to big rooftop tanks, and narrow pipes fed it down to homes
facts.note: 1974: illegal wells under houses, near open sewers (Lords c.464); wells chlorinated daily by the Urban Services Department (c.472)

facts.claim: Young people carried water for elderly residents for 50 cents a load
Plastic water pipes ran across the alleys and leaked; residents carried umbrellas against the drips
Light and power were taken from the mains by illegal connections; bare cables hung in festoons over the alleys

sources.loc: c.464 (Kennet); c.472 government calls the installation hazardous

facts.claim: The kaifong association arranged meters with the power company and residents helped run the wiring; broken cables were left and new ones added, shading the lanes
Fluorescent tubes lit the lanes around the clock because daylight rarely reached street level
With no proper collection, bulky rubbish (TVs, furniture, mattresses) was hauled up and dumped on the roofs
Government services in 1974: a sweeping team, refuse bins, public latrines, pest control, ditches cleared twice daily since 1973, pumphouses being installed
The government delivered mail into the city
Resident night-watch teams patrolled calling out fire warnings
In a fire in a rattan shop, a family on the 6th floor escaped by crossing from the 3rd floor to the next block's corridor, handing a baby across
Population when the 1898 Convention excluded the city
After the British attack of 14 Apr 1899 only the mandarin and about 150 residents remained
Squatters in the walled city
Official census counts (probably undercounts)
Municipal figure of 27,000 came from counting windows; officials privately put it at 45,000
Semi-official estimates
The government survey of 14 Jan 1987 counted about 33,000 residents: the best anchor figure
facts.note: We cite the survey via secondary sources; the survey itself is not online

facts.claim: Widely reported figure of about 50,000; some informal estimates wrongly included Sai Tau Tsuen
Households and premises: more than 8,000 households (HK01); about 10,700 households and 8,500 businesses (This House)
facts.note: Check against the 1987 clearance survey figures

facts.claim: Density at the 1987 count
A social worker estimated 10-20% of residents were illegal immigrants
About 700 industrial premises, many of them tiny metal fabrication shops, mostly between the ground and 5th floors
Ground floors held factories: looms, light engineering, metal goods, carpentry, food preparation; no law covered conditions
Fish balls, barbecued and roast meat and other foods were made in premises with little or no sanitation
Fish ball factories were unlicensed and ran round the clock
Popular claim that up to 80% of Hong Kong's fish balls came from the city
facts.note: No primary source found; present as a popular claim

facts.claim: Unlicensed doctors and dentists practised without fear of prosecution, mainly China-trained practitioners whose qualifications Hong Kong did not recognise
Over 150 dental clinics at their peak
Dental clinics clustered along the city's edge (Tung Tau Tsuen Road frontage)
Restaurants and cafes served dog meat, illegal elsewhere in Hong Kong
Lane businesses included tailors, cobblers, appliance repair, plastic moulding, grocery stores, bone-setting clinics, barbers and restaurants
Rents were about a third below the rest of Kowloon (government housing was cheaper still)
Monthly room rent
facts.note: Undated in the graphic; treat with care

facts.claim: A whole unit rented for about $800 a month in 1979
No rates, ground tax or real-estate tax were paid
There were no land deeds: sales were recorded on handwritten receipts, witnessed and stamped by the kaifong association
The kaifong association (from a 1963 anti-demolition committee) settled disputes and registered land titles outside the colony's courts
Compensation totalled about HK$2.7 billion (US$350 million), roughly HK$82,000 per person
facts.note: Baltimore Sun 1992: 'more than $300 million' (currency unclear)

facts.claim: Triads 14K and Sun Yee On controlled brothels, gambling parlours and opium dens from the 1950s
Police entered only in large groups and made few raids
A 1959 murder trial ruled that Hong Kong had jurisdiction in the city
More than 40 opium and heroin dens when Jackie Pullinger arrived (from 1966)
Vice concentrated along Lung Shing Road and Kwong Ming Street, including a striptease club and cinema
More than 3,500 police raids, over 2,500 arrests and over 1,800 kg of drugs seized; triad power waned afterwards
In the same debate one peer described triad extortion and drug trafficking while the government called the enclave relatively crime-free and patrolled
The district police commander declared crime under control
Triad societies still operated in the lanes; police patrols had only recently begun and were infrequent
Most residents were not involved in crime; former residents remember a close, poor but generally happy community
Patrols and police accompanied women returning home at night
By the 1992 evictions the brothels, opium dens and gambling clubs were gone
Charities and churches worked inside after 1963; Jackie Pullinger ran a youth club and later (1981) founded the St Stephen's Society for addicts
Roofs held TV antennas, clothes lines, water tanks and rubbish, linked by ladders; they were gathering places where children played and did homework
Rooftops were also used for exercise, playgrounds and pigeon racing
People hung washing, sat on bamboo chairs, chatted and watched the city lights from the roofs
Several schools and kindergartens, some run by groups such as the Salvation Army
In the middle stood the free school (義學, the oldest building), the youth centre and the old people's centre
During the Yu Lan (Hungry Ghost) Festival residents burned paper offerings in the lanes
Runway 13 approach: an IGS beam led planes over Kowloon City toward Checkerboard Hill, then a low 47-degree right turn (about 650 ft at the start, about 140 ft at the end) onto short final
Night curfew at Kai Tak
Residents lived with serious aircraft noise
Aircraft passed only a few feet above the top storeys
facts.note: Exaggerated; use real approach geometry for animation

facts.claim: A Song dynasty military outpost managed the salt trade here
About 30 guards were stationed at the site
A small coastal fort was set up after Tung Lung Fort was abandoned
The walled fort and Yamen were completed in response to British Hong Kong (Treaty of Nanking 1842)
The Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory (9 Jun 1898) leased the New Territories but excluded the walled city
British forces took the city on 14 Apr 1899; Qing officials left
An attempt to clear squatters in January 1948 failed and Britain adopted a hands-off policy
A January 1950 fire destroyed over 2,500 huts, home to nearly 3,500 families and 17,000 people
facts.note: May cover the wider Kowloon City squatter area

facts.claim: A clearance attempt was halted after protests from Beijing
The Sino-British Joint Declaration set Hong Kong's 1997 return and laid the groundwork for demolition
On 14 Jan 1987 the demolition was announced; police and Housing Department staff sealed the city and surveyed every household
Holdouts were forcibly evicted between Nov 1991 and Jul 1992
Demolition ran from 23 Mar 1993 to Apr 1994, by hand and machine rather than explosives (near the airport)
Kowloon Walled City Park was completed in Aug 1995 and opened by Governor Chris Patten on 22 Dec 1995
City outline measured on the May 1987 survey sheet (outer wall lines of the edge buildings)
facts.note: Sits at the top of the published 2.6-2.8 ha range. The outline follows building walls, so it excludes perimeter roads

facts.claim: City length and width measured on the 1987 sheet along its long axis (about 25 degrees north of east)
facts.value: 210-218 m long, 123-144 m wide (wider at the east end)
facts.note: The site is a trapezoid, so single figures like 213 x 126 m are averages

facts.claim: Building plots outlined on the May 1987 sheet
facts.value: 482 building plots, 454 with a printed number (plus the Yamen halls, 4 temple plots, 2 latrines, a shrine)
facts.note: A plot is an outlined lot, not necessarily one tower: some carry number ranges (e.g. 65-59) and 27 traced regions held several numbers divided by faint lines

facts.claim: Size of building plots on the 1987 sheet
facts.value: median 32 m2 (10% under 12 m2, 10% over 85 m2)
facts.note: Footprint per plot; floor area per unit was smaller (see unit-size)

facts.claim: Ground-level lanes measured between building outlines on the 1987 sheet
facts.value: median width 1.8 m (10% under 1.1 m, 10% over 2.8 m); about 5,900 m2, a fifth of the site
facts.note: Wall-line to wall-line at 1:1000 (line weight ~0.5 m), so +-0.3 m. Upper floors often bridged over the lanes

facts.claim: The ground sloped down from north-west to south-east
facts.value: about 17 m above Principal Datum at the north edge, 15 m north of the Yamen, 12 m at the Yamen, 8 m at the south-east edge; Tung Tau Tsuen Road 22-23 m
facts.note: The 1961 values are printed in feet (55.70, 48.50, 25.14, 25.30) and were read by eye

facts.claim: Yamen hall footprints traced from the 2024 survey
facts.value: about 49 x 16 m overall; 6 roofed parts totalling about 490 m2
facts.note: The 1987 and 2024 sheets place the Yamen about 1.5 m apart, a measure of how far the sheets' georeferencing drifts

facts.claim: The 1989 edition of sheet 11-NE-11A leaves the city blank, labelled 'Kowloon Walled City', with no plots inside
facts.note: So 1987 is the last edition that maps the plots

facts.claim: Storeys counted on four buildings in Lambot's 1989 aerial (window rows, roof to base)
facts.note: Matching each building to its plot used a camera solved from the base corners; a neighbouring plot is possible. Shows heights varied by several storeys along the edge, not a uniform 14

facts.claim: Clearance claimant case files kept by the Government Records Service
facts.value: 8,823 files: about 7,900 household claims, 690 business claims, 85 property-owner claims
facts.note: Household files are catalogued by (redacted) name only; business and owner files give address, floor and often the business name and trade

facts.claim: Businesses named in the clearance claims, by trade (classified by us from their names)
facts.value: 565 named businesses: 75 stores/trading, 74 food factories, 52 dentists, 44 plastics, 35 metalwork, 33 clinics, 28 leather/shoes/bags, 25 textiles, 20 restaurants, 15 electrical, 9 roast meat, 101 trade unclear
facts.note: Only 52 dentistry businesses filed claims, against the popular 'over 150 dental clinics'; some dentists may have closed before clearance or filed under a personal name

facts.claim: Floors named in business claims
facts.value: G/F 316, mezzanine or cockloft 26, 1/F 84, 2/F 50, 3/F 31, 4/F 17, 5/F 7, 6/F and above 24
facts.note: Supports the SCMP's 'mostly between the ground and 5th floors'. Some businesses ran from flats as high as 12/F

facts.claim: Streets named in dentists' claims
facts.value: Tung Tau Tsuen Road 18, Lung Chun Road 12, Lung Shing Road 12, Lo Yan Street 1 (17 give no address)
facts.note: All three main streets are the outer roads, so the claims confirm that dentists clustered on the city's edge

facts.claim: The survey's 'West City Road' is the claims' 'Sai Shing Road' (西城路, Cantonese for West City)
facts.note: Likewise 'Lo Yan Back Street' in the claims probably corresponds to the survey's 'Alms House Back Street' (inferred from the names)

facts.claim: Units in the model's illustrative floor layouts
facts.value: 8,898 units, of which 8,219 homes and about 680 businesses; about 4 people per home if 33,000 residents
facts.note: Layouts are illustrative (flats of 15-28 m2, median 19 m2); the home count falls inside the reported 8,000-10,700 households

facts.claim: The city wall's line traced on the 1922 survey
facts.value: about 660 m around, enclosing about 2.7 ha
facts.note: Traced by eye; the wall line runs close to the 1987 city outline, so the towers rose on roughly the fort's ground

facts.claim: One resident's family of eight (parents, grandmother, five children) rented the upper floor of a two-storey tin-sheet house of about 400 sq ft; the roof leaked whenever it rained
A couple's 5th-floor flat in a rear block, bought cheaply second-hand in the 1980s, had no windows at all
Homes doubled as workshops: mothers took in piecework, children assembled toys after school, and many small workshops (plastic flowers, garments, noodles, fish balls) were run by one family
When a home lost power, the neighbours upstairs lowered a plug on its cable to share theirs
Well water was badly polluted and mostly undrinkable; drinking water came from eight street taps
1987 plots whose outline is already drawn on each earlier survey sheet (outline within 0.5 m, after aligning each sheet)
facts.value: 266 of 497 plots drawn on every sheet from 1961; the rest appear from 1968 to 1987
facts.note: Lot lines persisted: a plot drawn in 1961 had a building of some kind, not necessarily the 1987 tower

facts.claim: First 1:1000 sheet that draws each building plot with the heavy line of a permanent building
facts.value: 228 by 1975, 22 from 1978, 31 from 1980, 2 from 1984, 64 from 1987; 150 only ever thin
facts.note: Measured from line width on the scans; dates the drawing, not the construction

facts.claim: 'CIP' (construction in progress) notes printed on the survey sheets inside the city
facts.value: 53 notes on 10 sheets, on 34 plots; 14 with a readable date (Nov 1971 to Jun 1978)
facts.note: Read with OCR; most dates are illegible on the scans

facts.claim: The fish-ball workshops had no air-conditioning
